F1.Q1: Cut sandstone flagstones — dressed rectangular slabs, warm ochre-tan, laid in an irregular running bond with recessed dark-brown mortar joints.
F1.Q1_WHY: In the lit corridor (x 375–439, y 0–405) the blocks have straight machined edges and square corners, not fractured or natural ones. Joints are a consistent 2–3px recess in a colder brown than the faces. Block sizes vary within the course — at y 210–240 the run is split into two stones of unequal width, at y 250–276 it is a single full-width slab — which is masonry coursing, not tiling. Colour is uniformly ochre with no mineral variation, so: sandstone or a soft limestone, quarried and dressed.
F1.Q2: North, up the corridor. **The ground played no part in that choice.** I picked north because the corridor is exactly one tile wide (measured: x 375 to 438, 64px) and the walls funnel me, and because south at y>405 is black at 1:1 and I can't see into it. If you deleted the walls and showed me only the flagstone, I could not tell you where the corridor is or which end I came from. That is a random choice dressed up as a decision.
F1.Q3: Nothing has happened to it. It is intact, level, complete and clean. No stone is cracked through, sunk, tilted, chipped at a corner, or missing. No stone has been replaced. No mortar has fallen out. There is no dirt, no staining, no spill, no rubble, no drift against the wall bases, no scuff. The condition is "recently laid, not yet used."
F1.Q3_WHY: Every mortar joint in the lit run reads full-depth and continuous — check y 139, y 209, y 236 across x 378–430; these are the highest-contrast lines in the whole floor and they are unbroken. The corridor mouth at (x 370–445, y 380–420), where a one-tile chokepoint meets an open room and every single person passing this level must step, has no threshold wear, no rounded corner on the jamb stone, no dishing, no debris — the bond simply continues across the doorway line as if nothing walks there. The only marks present anywhere are two texture motifs (see Q4), and they are distributed evenly rather than concentrated where feet would go, which makes them read as quarry tool-marks, not as wear.
F1.Q4:
Yes, three things.

1. **A "/" diagonal hatch motif**, same angle, same size, same placement on the upper-left of the face, reused down the corridor: (x 380–402, y 112–136), (x 378–404, y 210–236), (x 378–412, y 298–328). Directional test confirms it — at (380–402, 112–136) the anti-diagonal difference is 5.95 against 12.77 down-diagonal, so those are genuinely parallel "/" lines, and they are the same "/" every time.
2. **A vertical-striation motif** (short vertical dashes), reused at (x 400–424, y 248–268) and (x 410–428, y 310–330). Vertical difference 2.61 and 1.90 against horizontal 8.29 and 6.34 — same stamp, twice.
3. **Per-stone flat tone stepping.** Sampling mean brightness down the corridor: y 224 → 168.6, y 284 → 96.6, y 124 → 137.4. The stone at y 224 is 50px from the lamp and reads 168; the stone at y 124 is also ~50px from the lamp and reads 137. That 30-level gap is not lighting, it is the stones being painted different flat values. At 1:1 the corridor reads as a stack of alternating light and dark flat rectangles, and my eye kept going back to that checkering rather than to anything on the stone.
F1.Q5:
**Made** — at the layout level, and I'll defend that. Vertical autocorrelation down the lit corridor (x 377–437, y 0–400) finds no meaningful period: lag 64 scores 25.75 against a 25.15 floor at lag 22, i.e. no tile repeat is detectable. The coursing genuinely varies stone to stone. Somebody laid this.

But it is made only in its joints. The faces are not authored at all — see Q7. And in the wider floor south of the corridor, horizontal autocorrelation has a sharp, unambiguous minimum at exactly dx = 64 (1.815, against 1.886 at 63 and 1.841 at 65, on a 2.08 baseline). So the layout was made and the surface was repeated.
F1.Q6:
YES. It is clean, consistent, correctly bonded, well-valued, and nothing in it is broken.

Merely competent, or genuinely good? **Merely competent.** It is the floor a good technician makes when told "stone corridor." It has no point of view, tells no story, and contains no single element I would remember five minutes after closing the image.
F1.Q7:
**Legible at 1:1:** the joints, and the flat tone of each stone. That is the entire list. The faces are blank. What I read at full size was tan rectangles of slightly differing value, separated by dark lines.

**Only appears once magnified:** the "/" diagonal hatch; the vertical striations; the slight tonal grading inside individual faces. All of it required 4–6x, and I had to go looking. That is hunting, not seeing.
F1.Q7_WHY:
Measured. Masking mortar out and taking face pixels only: (388–428, 118–142) std 9.08 on mean 148.5 — that is the hatched stone, the strongest face in the corridor. (384–424, 214–238) std **1.78** on mean 175.4. (388–428, 252–276) std 3.38. (384–428, 300–326) std 4.14. (388–428, 72–92) std 3.01. A standard deviation of 2–4 grey levels on a 140-level face is not visible on a phone. Separately, ranking every 6x6 patch of the corridor by local contrast, the top twelve are all either the wall boundary at x 434 or the mortar rows at y 139 / 209 / 236 — the joints carry effectively all the contrast in this floor, and the median face patch scores 10 against the sprite's 84.

Checked at 1:1: (375–439, 60–140), (375–439, 205–340), (370–445, 380–420), (375–439, 0–55).
Magnified: (360–460, 0–160) at 6x, (360–460, 190–410) at 6x, (370–445, 0–405) at 4x, (330–490, 350–450) at 5x, (180–750, 400–600) at 2x with gamma lift.
F1.Q8: **Laid last year, and nobody has walked on it yet.** It reads as one age everywhere — corridor and room mouth are indistinguishable in condition.
F1.Q8_WHY:
The evidence is what is absent from specific places where four centuries would have to show. At the corridor mouth (370–445, 380–420) — a one-tile pinch that every soul, every orc patrol, every load of salvaged timber must funnel through — the jamb stones have square unbroken corners and the floor across the threshold is flush and unmarked. Along the corridor centreline (395–420, y 60–340) the tone is not distinguishable from the corridor edges (378–392) beyond what the lamp falloff accounts for, so there is no polished or dished walking track. Every joint from y 15 to y 370 is at full recess depth; not one is packed with grime or spalled open. And the two texture motifs (Q4) are distributed at even density regardless of position — the stone at the doorway carries the same amount of mark as the stone at the far end. Wear concentrates; this does not, so it is not wear.

For a place in continuous heavy use since before anyone's records begin, held by a company that repairs everything with rope and driven pins and does not care how it looks, this floor is the wrong age by four hundred years. There is not one pin, one patch, one plank, one wrong-coloured replacement slab anywhere in the lit ground.
F1.Q9: The route runs **north–south**, and **I read it entirely off the walls.** The ground told me nothing.
F1.Q9_WHY: Along the route — (375–439, 0–150) and (375–439, 205–400) — the coursing runs horizontally, perpendicular to travel, in stacked bands. It does the same thing in the room I rejected, at (185–640, 410–600), at the same scale, in the same bond, with the same joint weight. There is no directional grain, no lengthwise slab, no kerb, no drain line, no centre track, nothing that runs *with* the corridor. The one place the ground had an obvious job to do is the mouth at (370–445, 395–415): the floor crosses from one-tile passage into open room and does not change by a single pixel. Same stone, same course height, same joint colour, no sill, no lip, no threshold slab. So the only difference between the ground I would walk and the ground I rejected is that pink placeholder blocks are sitting on top of the latter. Take those away and the floor is silent about its own shape.
F1.Q10:
**They all look the same.** Two openings are within the light: the corridor continuing north off-frame at (375–439, y 0), and the corridor mouth opening south into the room at (375–439, y ≈405). The ground in front of both is identical — same bond, same joint depth, same absence of wear, same absence of debris. Nothing tells me one is a daily route and the other is sealed and forgotten. In a place that is a filing system for souls, where traffic *is* the story, the floor has no traffic in it.

---
F1.CULL: Walked daily for centuries, yet no wear track, no repair, no damage — the floor reads brand new.
F1.FLIP LIST:
- Put a wear track down the corridor centreline (x 395–420, y 0–400): lighter, joint-softened stone through the middle, dirtier and sharper-edged at the wall margins — legible at 1:1, not on magnification.
- Break the threshold at the corridor mouth (370–445, 395–415): round the jamb corners, dish the crossing stone, drop a step or a sill so the ground itself says a passage begins here.
- Retire the two reused stamps and give the corridor 4–6 genuinely different events at 1:1 scale — one cracked-through slab, one sunk stone with a lipped edge, one missing slab showing what's beneath, one replacement in the wrong stone.
- Add the orcs' repairs: at least one driven-pin plate or salvaged timber patch across a failed slab in the lit run, cut in at the wrong angle and not cleaned up.
- Raise face detail from std 2–4 to something that survives at 1:1 — grit, drift and staining collecting along the wall lines at x 378–384 and x 428–434, so the joints stop being the only thing carrying contrast.

---

Where this goes next: the joint work is the strong part and is worth keeping as-is. Every fix above is additive on top of it — none require relaying the bond. The one that buys the most per pixel is the wear track, because it fixes Q2, Q9 and Q10 simultaneously: it makes the ground navigable without the walls.

F2.Q1: Cut sandstone or warm limestone blocks, laid in irregular courses with recessed mortar joints. Roughly two blocks across the corridor width, block faces about 30×26 px.
F2.Q1_WHY: The lit floor occupies x 377–438, y 0–390 (measured, not eyeballed — that's the full tan extent). Within it the joints are darker recessed lines, not drawn outlines, and the block sizes are unequal course to course — compare the single wide block at y≈290–330 spanning nearly the full corridor against the two-block course at y≈150–190. The colour sits at r>g>b with a mid-tone around lum 115–129, a dry warm stone, not brick, not tile, not flag. Below y≈400 the material changes to a cold grey flagstone, but that is beyond the lamp and I'm not scoring it.
F2.Q2:
South, down into the dark room — and the ground did not choose it for me. I chose it because the corridor visibly opens into a larger space at y≈400 and going north just leaves the frame. That's layout reading, not ground reading.

I checked for a ground reason and there isn't one. I ran the corridor's column luminance with the per-row lighting removed: the only structure is symmetric darkening at both walls (x 377 at −28, x 437 at −46) and a dip at x 407–409 that is a mortar joint. There is no centre lane, no polish, no scuff darkening, no debris drift, nothing that says feet went this way rather than that way.
F2.Q3: It has been broken, once, and never touched since. A single fracture runs the entire lit length. Twice along its run the stone has failed outright and spalled into a shallow crater. Nothing has been swept, filled, pinned or patched.
F2.Q3_WHY:
- The crack: a continuous dark fissure at x≈405–422 from y≈20 to y≈390, unbroken across the whole visible corridor. It crosses course boundaries rather than stopping at them — visible at y≈145, y≈235, y≈285 where it steps over a joint and keeps going. That is authored, not stamped.
- Spall one: x≈400–435, y≈240–275 — a ragged blown-out patch where the crack widens and the block face has come away in chunks.
- Spall two: x≈405–440, y≈345–375 — same failure, at the corridor mouth.
- What's absent is louder. Four hundred years of orcs who repair everything with rope, pins, hide and timber, and there is not one repair on this floor. No driven pin, no timber baulk, no packed rubble in the fracture. The floor is damaged but nobody has ever been on it with a hammer.
F2.Q4:
Yes, two things.

First, the crack itself — but as a pull, not a fault. It's the only incident in 62×390 px of lit floor, so the eye has nowhere else to land and keeps going back to x≈410, y 20–390. That's a symptom of the faces being empty around it.

Second, and this is beyond the lamp so I'm reporting it rather than judging it: the room floor at y 400–600 has one blast crater per tile, at a metronomic cadence. I measured the centres in the band y 455–500: x = 284, 332, 403, 469, 547, 601, 638, 702 — gaps of 48, 71, 66, 78, 54, 37, 64. That clusters on the 64 px grid pitch. The band at y 535–585 does the same. At 1:1 they read as a dim row of evenly spaced dark discs marching across the screen. If that decal density carries into lit areas it will read as wallpaper.
F2.Q5:
Made. The corridor is not tiled art.

I autocorrelated the lit floor strip (x 377–438, y 0–390) vertically after removing the lighting gradient. There is no peak at 64, 128 or any other period — correlation decays monotonically from 0.54 at shift 8 and never recovers. A repeated tile would spike. The horizontal autocorrelation of the room floor does the same: no periodic spike. Block-hash comparison at 32 px and 64 px found duplicate groups only in fully black regions.

The clinching evidence is the crack. A single fracture holding its identity for 370 px across five or six courses cannot come out of a tile set; it was drawn onto this specific corridor.
F2.Q6:
YES.

Merely competent. Not genuinely good. The silhouette work is clean, the courses are properly irregular, the crack is real authored damage — that clears the commercial bar. But the block faces carry nothing at 1:1, there is exactly one narrative event in the entire lit floor, and the floor tells me nothing about who uses it. Competent stonework, no authorship.
F2.Q7:
Legible at 1:1: mortar joints, the crack, and a soft warm-to-cool gradient across each face that reads as a bevel. That is the complete list. The spall at y≈345–375 is present at 1:1 but reads as an indistinct dark smudge — I could not tell it was broken stone until I magnified. **The block faces themselves are blank at 1:1.** Flat tan with a bevel.

Only on magnification: fine diagonal scratch hatching, and a low-amplitude mottle in the stone.

I want to be exact about the hunting. I did not see the scratches, suspect them, and confirm them. I magnified to 5× for other reasons and they appeared. At 1:1 I had read those same faces as empty. That is hunting.
F2.Q7_WHY:
- Checked at 1:1 (native strip, x 374–442, y 0–400): faces at x 380–405 / y 190–212; x 380–405 / y 300–322; x 416–436 / y 60–84; x 380–405 / y 100–124. Joints and crack read. Faces read blank.
- Only on 5× magnification: diagonal scratches at x≈380–405, y≈214–234 and x≈380–408, y≈300–330; the mottle across all faces; the rubble structure inside both spalls.
- The numbers agree. A clean face at x 382–404, y 300–322 measures σ 8.8 — near flat. The faces that measure high (σ 43 at y 190–212) are high only because the crack or a joint clips them, not because the face has content.
F2.Q8:
Old — a few centuries at least, and worked stone rather than ancient. But I'm reading that off the fiction and off the damage, not off the stone. Honestly: the floor gives me a **broken** signal, not an **old** signal, and those are different things.

It reads as one age everywhere. No patching, no differing courses, no younger stone set into older, no zone where the wear is deeper. Uniform throughout.

What ages a floor is accumulation — hollows worn into the tread line, joints packed with centuries of dirt, edges rounded off, previous repairs weathered to a different tone than the repairs on top of them. None of that is here. The mortar joints are as crisp at the corridor mouth as at the top of the frame. The block edges are sharp. Strip out the crack and this stone could have been laid last year.
F2.Q8_WHY: Damage evidence from x 405–422 / y 20–390 (the crack) and the two spalls at y 240–275 and y 345–375. Uniformity checked by measuring dark-pixel fraction in 65 px bands down the corridor — the variation that comes back (10.7% to 37.5%) tracks the lamp falloff, not the damage, so there is no age gradient to read. Joint crispness checked at y≈232 and y≈393.
F2.Q9:
The route runs north–south, and **I read it off the walls, not off the ground.**

The corridor is bounded at x 377 and x 438 by unbroken wall for the entire lit height. That's what tells me this is a north–south passage. The floor inside those bounds is the same floor at the top of the frame as at the bottom.

The ground told me nothing. There is one linear feature aligned with the corridor — the crack at x≈410 — and it is direction-shaped, but it's a structural failure, not a path. It doesn't tell me north from south, and it doesn't tell me where the walking happens. If you rotated the floor 180° I could not detect it from the ground.
F2.Q9_WHY: Route regions along the lit corridor: y 0–65, 65–130, 130–195, 195–260, 260–325, 325–390, all at x 379–437. I looked for a difference between them and found none that survives correcting for the lamp. I rejected everything at x < 377 and x > 438 on wall geometry alone, not on ground evidence. Within the corridor there is no interior region I can reject — the whole width looks equally walked, which for a route in daily use is exactly the thing that's missing. A trafficked corridor should have a lane and two dead margins. This has one uniform surface wall to wall.
F2.Q10:
They look the same.

Two openings are lit: the corridor continuing north off the top edge (x 377–438, y 0–15) and the corridor mouth opening south into the room (x 377–438, y 385–400). Judging only the ground in front of each: the north approach is clean stone with the crack running through it; the south approach is clean stone with the crack running through it plus one spall. No difference in dirt, no difference in polish, no threshold worn hollow, no debris pushed to one side, no scuffing fanning out from either mouth.

I initially wondered whether damage clustered toward the south mouth. I measured it and it doesn't — the apparent gradient was the lamp. There is nothing here that ranks these two openings.

---
F2.CULL: Block faces are blank at 1:1 and the ground records no traffic — a walked route that nobody walks.
F2.FLIP LIST:
- Put a traffic lane in the corridor: darken and smooth a soft band roughly x 392–424 running the full length, leaving the wall margins at x 377–391 and x 425–438 lighter and grittier. Right now the floor is uniform wall to wall.
- Give the block faces something readable at 1:1 — pitting, staining, a scored line — at a contrast that survives without magnifying. The current scratches at x 380–405 / y 214–234 measure σ 8.8 against the face and are invisible at native scale.
- Put orc repair on the damage. Driven pins across the crack at x≈410, or a timber baulk and packed rubble in the spall at y 345–375. A floor in a place defined by four hundred years of repairing has no repairs on it.
- Break the one-crater-per-tile cadence in the room floor (y 400–600) — measured centres land on the 64 px pitch. Cluster them, run some across joints, leave whole tiles empty.
- Differentiate the two mouths. Grind and darken the ground in front of one (x 377–438, y 385–400) and leave the other with settled dust, so the ground says which way people go.
